comparison: Both evaluate gene editing success (C16-C20) and phenotype generation (C2-C3). OpenEval finds strong support with specific editing efficiency data. Peer reviewers accept the gene editing success but note 'the data provided do not demonstrate any significant difference' regarding sgRNA design improvements, showing partial agreement on technical success but disagreement on claimed optimization.

Both address the mutant phenotype and molecular characterization (C2-C4, C119). OpenEval finds evidence well-documented across generations. Peer reviewers accept the phenotype but note it differs from typical double-muscle phenotypes, showing agreement on data quality but different interpretation of phenotypic significance.

Both evaluate muscle fiber characteristics showing hyperplasia (C5, C21-C25, C31). OpenEval finds strong quantitative support with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers acknowledge the histological data showing increased fiber number and decreased size, accepting the hyperplasia characterization despite noting it differs from expected double-muscle phenotype.

Both address FGF5+/- control data (C26, C120). OpenEval finds this effectively isolates gene contributions. Peer reviewers implicitly accept the finding but note that 'the use of FGF5 knockout sheep complicates the ability to accurately decipher the unique aspects associated with targeting only myostatin,' showing agreement on data but concern about experimental design complexity.

Both evaluate carcass composition and meat quality claims (C32-C34). OpenEval finds quantitative support for agricultural value without quality compromise. Peer reviewers explicitly critique this, stating 'the data provided did not demonstrate a significant improvement in meat production, quality or quantity,' showing fundamental disagreement on practical significance despite similar underlying data.

Both address cell proliferation data (C35-C39). OpenEval finds strong support from multiple complementary assays. Peer reviewers do not challenge the proliferation measurements themselves, showing agreement on the cellular characterization data quality.

Both evaluate differentiation inhibition claims (C40-C44). OpenEval finds consistent evidence across multiple markers and time points. Peer reviewers accept the in vitro differentiation data showing smaller myotubes, demonstrating agreement on the cellular phenotype observations.

Both address pathway enrichment and FOSL1 identification (C45-C50). OpenEval finds support from RNA-seq analysis with caveat about verification. Peer reviewers express significant skepticism, stating 'RNA-Seq data demonstrated that hundreds of different genes were either upregulated or down-regulated, but the authors chose to only focus on FOSL1,' questioning whether findings are 'co-incidental and not causative,' showing major disagreement on interpretation.

Both evaluate FOSL1 expression patterns (C47-C50). OpenEval finds consistent temporal expression during differentiation. Peer reviewers question the selective focus on FOSL1 from broader RNA-seq data, showing agreement on expression data but disagreement on its significance.

Both address FOSL1-MyoD1 interaction and binding (C53-C60). OpenEval finds well-established mechanistic chain from binding to functional inhibition. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'the authors provide evidence using in vitro experiments that Fosl1 regulates myogenesis' but emphasize 'the cellular and molecular mechanism remain inadequate to conclude whether Fosl1 indeed acts downstream of myostatin,' showing agreement on direct binding data but disagreement on broader mechanistic interpretation.

Both evaluate MEK-ERK-FOSL1 pathway activation (C6, C61-C66). OpenEval finds coordinated changes provide evidence for pathway activation. Peer reviewers state 'the authors focus on the MEK-ERK-FOSL1 pathway and suggest this is the key pathway/mechanism resulting in the phenotype observed... However, they provide very little "significant" evidence to support this,' showing agreement on Western blot data but strong disagreement on causal interpretation.

Both address the integrated mechanistic model (C6-C7 for OpenEval, C6 for peer). OpenEval finds the model supported by multiple lines of evidence including gain/loss-of-function. Peer reviewers question the strength of evidence for the proposed mechanism, showing fundamental disagreement on whether the data support the mechanistic conclusions.

Both evaluate FOSL1 overexpression experiments (C73-C78). OpenEval finds comprehensive support across multiple assays for FOSL1's inhibitory role. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'the authors provide evidence using in vitro experiments that Fosl1 regulates myogenesis,' accepting the gain-of-function data while questioning connection to in vivo phenotype.

Both address FOSL1 knockdown experiments (C79-C84). OpenEval finds strong bidirectional evidence from complementary loss-of-function data. Peer reviewers accept these as part of in vitro evidence but maintain 'the cellular and molecular mechanism remain inadequate to conclude whether Fosl1 indeed acts downstream of myostatin,' showing agreement on experimental results but disagreement on mechanistic conclusions.

Both evaluate pharmacological validation of ERK1/2-FOSL1 axis (C85-C90). OpenEval finds bidirectional evidence with caveat about compound specificity. Peer reviewers do not specifically challenge the pharmacological data, accepting it as supporting the ERK1/2-FOSL1 connection while maintaining broader concerns about the pathway being the primary mechanism.

Both address Ca2+ signaling pathway claims (C8, C91-C95). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting correlative data without direct causal demonstration. Peer reviewers similarly note 'the strength of evidence relating to the muscle phenotype and underlying cellular and molecular mechanism remains incomplete,' showing strong agreement that causal evidence is lacking.

Both evaluate serum regulation and receptor expression (C67-C72). OpenEval finds evidence for non-cell-autonomous effects though specific factors remain unidentified. Peer reviewers do not specifically challenge these findings, accepting them as part of the characterization, showing general agreement on this aspect.

Both address temporal MSTN expression patterns (C27-C28). OpenEval finds support but raises questions about phenotype maintenance if expression normalizes. Peer reviewers do not specifically challenge this data, which is accepted as part of phenotypic characterization, showing implicit agreement.
